paper.title_en: When Graph Autoencoders Look the Wrong Way: Complexity Bias and Simple Baselines in Unsupervised Anomaly Detection on the LHC Olympics 2020 Dataset
paper.abstract_en: Graph autoencoders (GAEs) trained only on background are a natural candidate for model-agnostic new-physics searches. I tested two of them on the LHC Olympics 2020 R&D dataset, where a W' -> XY -> (qq)(qq) dijet resonance is hidden in QCD background. The first is a node-level GAE that scores per-particle reconstruction error. The second encodes the whole event, reconstructs it with a set decoder and a Chamfer loss, and offers three scores: reconstruction error, latent k-nearest-neighbour distance and latent Gaussian-mixture likelihood. The decision criterion was fixed before looking at any test result. Neither model beats simple label-free observables. The node-level model reaches an AUC of 0.483 +/- 0.005 with max-reduction and 0.781 with mean-reduction; all three event-level scores are inverted, with AUCs between 0.401 and 0.436, stable across seeds, nine ablations, and signal-contaminated training. By contrast, the mean transverse momentum per particle, <pT> = HT/N, reaches 0.811, and -tau21 of the leading jet reaches 0.801. Correlation and binned analyses indicate that the latent-density scores track event complexity: the signal has fewer, harder particles than QCD and is therefore placed in dense regions of the learned manifold. The benchmark code is public, and I suggest <pT> as a standard reference baseline for unsupervised methods on this dataset.
